headline: High risk of data leakage and capability conflict: shared filesystem plus broad egress and shell execution make the pair unsafe by default.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Both agents can read and write the filesystem, so untrusted document content from agent_a can be placed where agent_b may later read it as shell input or instructions. Agent_b also processes stdin/stdout and shell commands, increasing the chance of content being interpreted operationally. No direct shared channel is documented, so this is inferred from overlapping file surfaces.
conditions: IF agent_a writes attacker-controlled document text into a shared directory that agent_b reads
IF agent_b consumes file contents or stdin as executable shell input without sanitization
mitigations: Separate working directories for the two agents
Disable automatic ingestion of files from agent_a into agent_b
Require explicit human review before agent_b executes content derived from agent_a
Use read-only mounts for agent_a outputs where possible

B_data_leakage.rationale: Agent_a touches documents, images, and text and can write files; agent_b reads filesystem contents and has broad network egress. That creates a plausible path for sensitive document content processed by agent_a to be forwarded by agent_b. The pair lacks documented isolation beyond generic containers/environments, so the leakage path is credible in default workflows.
conditions: IF agent_a processes sensitive documents into a shared filesystem location
IF agent_b reads those files and transmits derived content over network egress
mitigations: Keep sensitive inputs out of any shared workspace
Restrict agent_b network egress to approved destinations only
Encrypt or redact outputs before agent_b can access them
Use separate service accounts and storage roots for each agent

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents can write the filesystem and spawn subprocesses; agent_b also executes shell commands. Agent_a supports multiple instances, while agent_b does not, so concurrent writes to shared paths can race and corrupt state. Because no locking or shared-workspace isolation is documented, the conflict is dangerous by default and can cause irreversible file loss or inconsistent outputs.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same writable directory
IF agent_b executes shell commands that modify files while agent_a is concurrently processing them
mitigations: Serialize access with a lock file or orchestrator mutex
Run one agent at a time for shared resources
Snapshot or version files before either agent mutates them

D_cascading_error.rationale: Agent_a is a document-processing system that can emit extracted text, while agent_b can run shell commands and act on filesystem contents. If agent_b treats agent_a's extracted output as authoritative without verification, parsing errors or hallucinated structure can cascade into incorrect commands or transformations. The interaction is inferred, but the downstream action-taking authority makes the blast radius meaningful.
conditions: IF agent_b uses agent_a's extracted text as direct shell input or script content
IF no verification step checks agent_a's output before agent_b acts on it
mitigations: Insert a validation step between extraction and execution
Require schema checks on agent_a outputs before agent_b consumes them
Log and diff agent_a outputs before any shell action
Limit agent_b to read-only review of agent_a results

E_compliance.rationale: Both profiles are open-source and show no explicit residency, certification, or retention commitments, so there is no documented compliance mismatch to score higher. The only concrete compliance-relevant surface is that agent_a processes documents and agent_b can read filesystem contents, but no regulated-data handling is stated. The other agent is cited because the pairwise workflow still determines exposure.
conditions: IF regulated data such as PHI or EU PII is introduced into the shared workflow
IF the operator requires a specific residency or retention policy not documented in either profile
mitigations: Avoid placing regulated data in the shared workspace
Document retention and deletion handling before deployment
Use separate environments for regulated and unregulated workloads
